title: Vitamins Depleted by Alcohol: What Drinking Drains and How to Refill
excerpt: Which vitamins and minerals alcohol depletes, how it happens, how much drinking it takes to cause a deficiency, warning signs, and how to safely replace what's lost.
metaDescription: Which vitamins and minerals alcohol depletes, from thiamine to magnesium and selenium, how much drinking it takes, warning signs, and how to refill safely.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** alcohol can lower your levels of several vitamins and minerals, mainly **thiamine (vitamin B1), folate, vitamin B6, magnesium, zinc, and to a lesser degree vitamins A, D, and C, potassium, phosphate, and selenium**. It does this in three ways: you absorb less from food, your liver stores and uses less, and your kidneys flush more out in urine. For someone who has a few drinks on the weekend and eats a reasonable diet, true deficiency is uncommon. The real risk builds with **regular heavy drinking, especially when drinking replaces meals**. One night out mostly costs you fluid, magnesium, potassium, and zinc through extra urination, which food and water usually replace within a day or two.

**The quick rules:** Eat a real meal before and after drinking. If you drink often, a basic B-complex or multivitamin at around 100% of the daily value is a sensible, low-risk backstop, and thiamine is the single most important nutrient to keep topped up. Don't megadose vitamin A, iron, or selenium to "make up" for drinking, because those three can do harm in excess, and alcohol makes vitamin A and iron riskier, not safer. If you have numbness, confusion, trouble walking, or unusual tiredness and you drink regularly, talk to a doctor and ask for blood work.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research on alcohol and nutrition. It is not a substitute for a doctor who knows your health history. **See a doctor if** you drink most days and notice numbness or tingling in your hands or feet, ongoing fatigue, pale skin, cracks at the corners of your mouth, frequent muscle cramps, or an irregular heartbeat. **Get urgent care right away** for sudden confusion, unsteady walking, or unusual eye movements or double vision in someone who drinks heavily; these can be signs of a serious thiamine deficiency that needs treatment within hours, not days. If you drink heavily every day and want to stop, talk to a doctor first, because stopping suddenly can cause dangerous withdrawal (shaking, sweating, a racing heart, seeing things, or seizures). In an emergency, call 911.

## How Alcohol Depletes Vitamins and Minerals

It helps to know the mechanism, because it explains which nutrients take the biggest hit and why a single night is a different story from a habit.

### 1. You absorb less from food

Alcohol irritates the lining of the stomach and small intestine. Heavy drinking can inflame that lining and interfere with the transport proteins your gut uses to pull certain vitamins into the bloodstream. Thiamine and folate are the classic examples: their absorption depends on active carriers that alcohol is known to impair. Heavy drinking can also affect the pancreas, which makes the enzymes you need to digest fat. Poor fat digestion means poorer absorption of the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, and K.

### 2. Your liver stores and activates less

Your liver isn't just a filter. It's a warehouse and a processing plant for nutrients. Many vitamins have to be converted by the liver into their active form before your body can use them, and the liver holds reserves of vitamins A, D, B12, and folate. When the liver is busy breaking down alcohol, or has been damaged by years of heavy drinking, it stores less and converts less. **Acetaldehyde**, the toxic by-product your body makes when it breaks down alcohol, also speeds the breakdown of the active form of vitamin B6.

### 3. Your kidneys flush more out

Alcohol blocks a hormone (vasopressin, also called antidiuretic hormone) that normally tells your kidneys to hold onto water. That's why you pee more when you drink. Along with the water, your kidneys lose more **magnesium, zinc, potassium, calcium, and phosphate**. This is the part that affects social drinkers after a single night, and it's also why vomiting or diarrhea after drinking makes mineral losses worse. Our guide to [electrolytes and alcohol](/never-hungover/electrolytes-and-alcohol) covers the fluid side in more detail.

### 4. Drinking often crowds out food

This one is less about chemistry and more about habits, but it may matter most. Alcohol has calories (about 7 per gram) but almost no vitamins or minerals. When drinks replace meals, or late-night eating leans toward fast food, intake drops at the same time absorption and losses get worse. Researchers have long noted that in heavy drinkers, poor diet and alcohol's direct effects work together, and it's hard to separate the two.

## The Vitamins Most Affected by Alcohol

Here's the nutrient-by-nutrient picture, starting with the ones that matter most.

| Nutrient | How alcohol affects it | What low levels can cause | Who's most at risk |
|---|---|---|---|
| Thiamine (B1) | Less absorbed, less stored, less activated | Fatigue, nerve problems, and in severe cases brain damage | Regular heavy drinkers with poor diet |
| Folate (B9) | Less absorbed, more lost in urine | Anemia, fatigue, pregnancy risks | Heavy drinkers; anyone who may become pregnant |
| Vitamin B6 | Faster breakdown of the active form | Anemia, nerve symptoms, mouth soreness | Heavy drinkers |
| Vitamin B12 | Absorption reduced by stomach damage | Anemia, numbness, memory problems | Long-term heavy drinkers, older adults |
| Vitamin A | Liver stores drained, but excess is toxic | Night vision problems, dry eyes | Heavy drinkers with liver disease |
| Vitamin D | Lower levels, poorer liver processing | Weak bones, low mood (possible) | Heavy drinkers, anyone with little sun |
| Vitamin C | Lower blood levels in heavy drinkers | Fatigue, slow healing, gum problems | Heavy drinkers who eat little fruit and veg |
| Magnesium | More lost in urine | Cramps, twitching, poor sleep, heart rhythm issues | Anyone after heavy drinking; daily drinkers |
| Zinc | Less absorbed, more lost in urine | Poor taste, slow healing, weaker immunity | Regular heavy drinkers |

### Thiamine (vitamin B1): the one that matters most

If you remember one nutrient from this article, make it thiamine. Your body only stores a small amount, enough for a few weeks, and alcohol hits it on every front: it lowers absorption from the gut, reduces how much the liver stores, and interferes with turning thiamine into its active form.

Your brain and nerves run on thiamine. Mild deficiency can look vague: tiredness, irritability, poor appetite, and trouble concentrating. More serious deficiency can cause nerve damage (tingling or burning in the feet) and, in severe cases, a medical emergency called **Wernicke's encephalopathy**, which shows up as confusion, unsteady walking, and abnormal eye movements. If it isn't treated quickly, it can lead to lasting memory problems (Korsakoff syndrome). Hospitals routinely give thiamine to people admitted with heavy alcohol use for exactly this reason.

For social drinkers, the practical takeaway is reassuring but worth acting on: thiamine is cheap, safe at normal doses, and found in many foods. Our full guide on [thiamine and alcohol](/never-hungover/thiamine-and-alcohol) covers doses and food sources.

### Folate (vitamin B9)

Alcohol reduces how much folate you absorb, how much your liver holds onto, and how much your kidneys keep. Low folate is one of the most common nutrient problems in heavy drinkers. It can cause a type of anemia where red blood cells are large and don't work well, which leaves you tired and short of breath.

Folate matters especially for anyone who could become pregnant, because adequate folate early in pregnancy lowers the risk of neural tube defects. There's also research linking the combination of regular drinking and low folate intake with a higher risk of some cancers, including colorectal and breast cancer, though this is observational and the alcohol itself is a known risk factor. See [folic acid and alcohol](/never-hungover/folic-acid-and-alcohol) for more.

### Vitamin B6

B6 helps you make red blood cells and brain chemicals. Acetaldehyde, the toxic by-product of alcohol breakdown, speeds up the breakdown of B6's active form, so heavy drinkers can run low even when their diet contains enough. Symptoms of deficiency include anemia, a sore tongue, cracked lips, and nerve symptoms. One caution: B6 is a vitamin where more is not better. Long-term high-dose B6 supplements can themselves cause nerve damage, so stick to normal amounts.

### Vitamin B12

B12 is a bit different. Your liver stores a large reserve, often enough for years, so deficiency develops slowly. Heavy drinking can still lower B12 over time, mainly by damaging the stomach lining, which is needed to absorb it. Confusingly, people with alcohol-related liver damage sometimes show *high* B12 on blood tests because damaged liver cells release their stores into the blood, so a normal or high number doesn't always mean your tissues have enough. Our guide to [vitamin B12 and alcohol](/never-hungover/vitamin-b12-and-alcohol) covers B12 shots and whether they help hangovers (there is no good evidence that they do).

### Vitamin A: depleted, but don't megadose

Heavy drinking drains vitamin A stores in the liver. You might think the answer is to take extra vitamin A. It isn't. Alcohol and high-dose vitamin A together are harder on the liver than either alone, because both are processed through overlapping liver pathways. Large trials in the 1990s that gave beta-carotene supplements to smokers found more lung cancer, not less, and the effect seemed stronger in people who drank more. The lesson is that vitamin A is one nutrient where trying to "replace" what alcohol takes can backfire. Get it from food (carrots, sweet potato, leafy greens, eggs), and if you take a multivitamin, choose one with moderate vitamin A, partly as beta-carotene, not a high-dose product.

### Vitamin D

Heavy drinkers tend to have lower vitamin D levels, likely due to a mix of poorer diet, less time outdoors, and the liver's reduced ability to process vitamin D into its circulating form. Since vitamin D helps you absorb calcium, low levels add to the bone-thinning effect of long-term heavy drinking. Most people can't tell if their vitamin D is low without a blood test. See [vitamin D and alcohol](/never-hungover/vitamin-d-and-alcohol) for more.

### Vitamin C, E, and K

- **Vitamin C:** blood levels tend to be lower in heavy drinkers, partly from diet and partly from increased use as an antioxidant. It's water-soluble and easy to replace with fruit and vegetables. There is no good evidence that a vitamin C shot or megadose prevents a hangover. Our [vitamin C and alcohol](/never-hungover/vitamin-c-and-alcohol) guide goes into the research.
- **Vitamin E:** often low in people with alcohol-related liver disease, again tied to poor fat absorption and diet.
- **Vitamin K:** problems with blood clotting in heavy drinkers usually come from liver damage (the liver makes clotting factors) rather than low vitamin K itself, so taking vitamin K doesn't fix them.

## The Minerals Alcohol Drains

Minerals are where a single night of drinking has the most noticeable effect, because the kidneys lose them quickly.

### Magnesium

Alcohol increases how much magnesium you lose in your urine, and this happens with every drinking session, not just over years. Low magnesium is very common in heavy drinkers. It can contribute to muscle cramps, twitching, poor sleep, anxiety, and, in more severe cases, heart rhythm problems. Blood tests don't always pick it up, because most of the body's magnesium sits inside cells and bone rather than in blood. For more, including which forms are easiest on the stomach, see [magnesium and alcohol](/never-hungover/magnesium-and-alcohol).

### Zinc

Alcohol lowers zinc absorption and increases zinc loss in urine. Zinc helps with immune function, wound healing, taste and smell, and the activity of alcohol dehydrogenase, one of the enzymes that breaks down alcohol. A 2019 survey study from researchers in the Netherlands found that people with higher dietary zinc intake reported somewhat less severe hangovers. That's an association, not proof that zinc pills help, but it's a reason to make sure your diet includes zinc-rich foods. Zinc supplements above about 40 mg a day for long periods can cause copper deficiency, so don't overdo them.

### Potassium and phosphate

Extra urination, vomiting, and diarrhea all pull potassium out of the body. Low potassium can cause weakness, cramps, and palpitations. Phosphate is also often low in heavy drinkers, and doctors watch it carefully in people being treated for heavy drinking, because levels can drop further when a malnourished person starts eating again. Bananas, potatoes, beans, yogurt, and coconut water are easy food sources of potassium. Our [potassium and alcohol](/never-hungover/potassium-and-alcohol) guide covers when a supplement makes sense (rarely, without a doctor).

### Selenium

Selenium is a trace mineral your body uses to make antioxidant enzymes, including one (glutathione peroxidase) that helps protect the liver from oxidative damage. Studies have found lower selenium levels in people with alcohol-related liver disease, and lower levels tend to track with more severe disease. What's less clear is whether supplements help. There is no good evidence that selenium supplements protect the liver from alcohol in people, and selenium has a narrow safety margin: the adult upper limit is 400 micrograms a day, and too much can cause hair loss, brittle nails, a garlic smell on the breath, and nerve problems. Two Brazil nuts can provide a full day's selenium, and a few too many every day can push you past the limit, so this is a nutrient best handled through ordinary food or a standard multivitamin.

### Iron: the exception

Iron is the odd one out. Alcohol doesn't drain iron; it tends to do the opposite. Regular drinking can increase how much iron your gut absorbs, and iron overload adds to liver damage in heavy drinkers. Some people can be low in iron from stomach bleeding, but **you shouldn't take iron supplements to "replace" what alcohol takes without a blood test showing you need it**. Our [iron and alcohol](/never-hungover/iron-and-alcohol) guide explains the details.

## Alcohol and Vitamin Deficiency: How Much Drinking Does It Take?

This is the question most people really want answered, and the honest answer is that there isn't a single number. Deficiency depends on how much you drink, how often, how well you eat, your age, and your health. But a few general points hold up.

**Moderate drinking with a good diet is unlikely to cause a deficiency.** US dietary guidelines define moderate drinking as up to two drinks a day for men and one for women. Someone in that range who eats regular meals with fruit, vegetables, whole grains, and protein is not the person deficiency research is about.

**Heavy, regular drinking is where the risk lives.** The US National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism describes heavy drinking as more than 4 drinks on any day or more than 14 a week for men, and more than 3 on any day or more than 7 a week for women. At that level, especially over months or years, the losses add up faster than most diets replace them.

**Binge nights cause short-term losses, not long-term deficiency.** A big night out increases urinary losses of magnesium, potassium, and zinc and leaves you dehydrated. That contributes to how you feel the next day, but it isn't the same as being deficient, and a couple of decent meals plus fluids generally restore the balance.

**Diet is the multiplier.** The same amount of alcohol does much more damage to nutrient status in someone who skips meals, eats mostly processed food, or is already low because of pregnancy, older age, a restrictive diet, or a digestive condition like celiac or Crohn's disease. Certain medications can also lower nutrient levels on their own; metformin and acid-reducing drugs can lower B12, for example.

## Signs Your Drinking May Be Affecting Your Nutrition

None of these symptoms prove a deficiency on their own, and many have other causes. But if you drink regularly and notice several of them, it's worth getting checked.

- Tiredness that doesn't go away with sleep
- Tingling, burning, or numbness in the hands or feet
- Muscle cramps, twitching, or weakness
- Pale skin or getting out of breath easily
- Cracks at the corners of the mouth or a sore, smooth tongue
- Slow-healing cuts, or getting sick more often
- Poor appetite or a reduced sense of taste
- Brittle nails or thinning hair
- Low mood, irritability, or trouble concentrating

## When to See a Doctor

> **Book a regular appointment if** you drink most days and have ongoing fatigue, numbness or tingling, frequent cramps, or any of the signs above. Ask about a blood test. A doctor might check a complete blood count (large red blood cells are a common clue to low folate or B12, and to heavy drinking itself), folate, B12, vitamin D, magnesium, and liver function. Be honest about how much you drink; it changes which tests are useful and how results are read.
>
> **Get urgent care right away** for confusion, unsteady walking, unusual eye movements or double vision, or a racing or irregular heartbeat in someone who drinks heavily. Severe thiamine deficiency and very low potassium or magnesium are treatable, but they need treatment fast.
>
> **If you drink heavily every day and want to cut back or stop, talk to a doctor first.** Stopping suddenly after a long stretch of heavy daily drinking can cause withdrawal, with shaking, sweating, anxiety, a racing heart, seeing or hearing things, or seizures. That can be dangerous, and doctors can make it safe. If symptoms like these start, get medical help. In an emergency, call 911.

## How to Replace What Alcohol Takes

The good news is that for most people, this part is simple and inexpensive.

### Start with food

A varied diet covers most of these nutrients. A few foods do a lot of the work:

- **Thiamine:** pork, whole grains, fortified cereals and bread, beans, lentils, sunflower seeds
- **Folate:** leafy greens, beans, lentils, asparagus, avocado, fortified grains
- **B6 and B12:** fish, poultry, meat, eggs, dairy, fortified cereals (B12 is found almost only in animal foods and fortified products)
- **Magnesium:** nuts, seeds, beans, whole grains, dark chocolate, spinach
- **Zinc:** shellfish (especially oysters), beef, pumpkin seeds, chickpeas
- **Potassium:** potatoes, bananas, beans, yogurt, avocado
- **Vitamin C:** citrus, berries, peppers, kiwi, broccoli
- **Selenium:** fish, eggs, poultry, whole grains, a small number of Brazil nuts

Eating before you drink also slows how fast alcohol reaches your bloodstream, which is a separate benefit. Our guide on [what to eat before drinking](/never-hungover/what-to-eat-before-drinking-alcohol-evidence-based-guide) has practical options, and [eggs for a hangover](/never-hungover/eggs-for-hangover) explains why eggs are a reasonable choice the morning after.

### A basic supplement is a reasonable backstop

If you drink regularly, a standard multivitamin or B-complex that provides around 100% of the daily value for most nutrients is a low-risk way to cover gaps. A few guidelines:

- **Choose moderate doses.** Megadose products don't fix depletion faster, and some nutrients (vitamin A, B6, iron, selenium, zinc) are harmful in excess.
- **Prioritize B vitamins, especially thiamine.** This is where alcohol's effect is clearest.
- **Skip the iron** unless a blood test shows you need it. Many multivitamins come in "iron-free" or men's versions.
- **Take it with food,** which helps with absorption and is easier on a stomach that's had a rough night.

Our guide on [multivitamins and alcohol](/never-hungover/multivitamin-and-alcohol) covers timing and whether to take one before or after drinking, and [vitamins for a hangover](/never-hungover/vitamins-for-hangover) compares what each one realistically does the next morning. For a fuller plan if you're cutting back after a period of heavy drinking, see our [alcohol recovery nutrition guide](/never-hungover/alcohol-recovery-nutrition-complete-healing-protocol-2025).

### After a big night

You don't need a special protocol after one night out. Drink water, eat a proper meal with some protein, starchy carbs, and fruit or vegetables, and include a salty and potassium-rich food or an electrolyte drink if you were sick or sweaty. That replaces most of what the night cost you.

### Cut back on the cause

Supplements can fill gaps, but they can't offset the effects of heavy drinking on the liver, gut, and brain. If you find you're worried about depletion because you drink most days, the single most effective step is drinking less. Even a few alcohol-free days a week give your gut and liver time to recover and your kidneys time to stop leaking minerals.

## Can Vitamin Depletion Make Hangovers Worse?

Probably a little, but it isn't the main cause. Hangovers are mostly driven by the body's inflammatory response to alcohol, poor sleep, acetaldehyde, dehydration, and the effects of congeners (other compounds in drinks, especially dark spirits). Mineral losses from extra urination can add to fatigue, headache, and muscle aches the next day.

The research tying specific vitamins to hangover severity is limited. The Dutch survey mentioned above found that people who ate more zinc and nicotinic acid (vitamin B3) reported milder hangovers, but it relied on self-reported diet and can't show cause and effect. There is no good evidence that taking a vitamin pill or IV drip the morning after cures a hangover, and many "hangover IV" claims go far beyond the research.

## Where DHM Fits In

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree, and it isn't a vitamin. It doesn't replace thiamine, magnesium, or anything else alcohol depletes. Its research is about alcohol itself: animal studies suggest it may help the body process alcohol and its by-products faster and support the liver, but human data are still limited, and there is no good evidence that it prevents nutrient depletion.

If you want to try DHM alongside good food and a basic multivitamin, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20), which also includes some B vitamins and electrolytes, and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. Check with your doctor first if you take any regular medication.
For a combined approach, our guide to [B-complex and alcohol](/never-hungover/b-complex-and-alcohol) covers taking the B vitamins together, and [zinc and alcohol](/never-hungover/zinc-and-alcohol) explains why zinc, a mineral rather than a vitamin, is another nutrient regular drinking tends to drain.

## The Bottom Line

- Alcohol lowers several nutrients by reducing absorption, limiting liver storage, and increasing losses in urine.
- **Thiamine** is the most important one to protect, followed by **folate, B6, magnesium, and zinc**.
- A single night out mainly costs fluid and minerals, which food and water replace. True deficiency usually comes from **regular heavy drinking combined with a poor diet**.
- Eat real meals, consider a moderate-dose multivitamin or B-complex if you drink often, and don't megadose vitamin A, iron, or selenium.
- Confusion, unsteady walking, or eye movement problems in a heavy drinker need urgent care. Persistent tingling, fatigue, or cramps are worth a blood test.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What vitamins does alcohol deplete?**

Alcohol most clearly lowers thiamine (vitamin B1), folate, and vitamin B6, and it can also reduce vitamins A, D, C, E, and B12 over time. Among minerals, it increases losses of magnesium, zinc, potassium, and phosphate, and heavy drinkers often have low selenium. Iron is the exception: regular drinking tends to increase iron absorption rather than drain it.

**Does alcohol cause vitamin deficiency?**

It can, but mostly with regular heavy drinking, especially when drinking replaces meals. Alcohol reduces absorption, limits how much the liver stores and activates, and increases losses in urine. Someone who drinks moderately and eats a varied diet is unlikely to become deficient. A single night out mainly costs fluid and minerals, which food and water replace within a day or two.

**What is the most important vitamin to take if you drink?**

Thiamine (vitamin B1). Your body stores only a few weeks' worth, and alcohol lowers its absorption, storage, and activation. Severe deficiency can cause a medical emergency called Wernicke's encephalopathy. A standard B-complex or multivitamin covers normal needs, and thiamine-rich foods include pork, whole grains, fortified cereals, beans, and lentils.

**Does alcohol deplete selenium?**

Studies have found lower selenium levels in people with alcohol-related liver disease, and lower levels tend to go with more severe disease. There is no good evidence that selenium supplements protect the liver from alcohol, and selenium is easy to overdo: the adult upper limit is 400 micrograms a day. Get it from fish, eggs, poultry, whole grains, or a standard multivitamin rather than a high-dose product.

**Should I take a multivitamin if I drink?**

If you drink regularly, a multivitamin or B-complex at around 100% of the daily value is a reasonable, low-risk backstop. Choose moderate doses, skip iron unless a blood test shows you need it, and take it with food. A supplement fills gaps but doesn't offset alcohol's effects on the liver, gut, and brain.

**Can I take extra vitamin A to replace what alcohol depletes?**

It's not a good idea. Heavy drinking drains vitamin A from the liver, but high-dose vitamin A and alcohol together are harder on the liver than either alone, and large trials found beta-carotene supplements raised lung cancer risk in smokers, especially those who drank more. Get vitamin A from food and keep any supplement to a moderate dose.

**How long does it take to restore vitamins after drinking?**

After a single night, a couple of good meals and fluids usually restore fluid and mineral balance within a day or two. After a long stretch of heavy drinking, rebuilding stores can take weeks to months depending on the nutrient, and a doctor may recommend specific supplements based on blood tests. B12 stores, in particular, build slowly.

**What are the signs of vitamin deficiency from alcohol?**

Common signs include ongoing tiredness, tingling or numbness in the hands or feet, muscle cramps, pale skin, cracks at the corners of the mouth, a sore tongue, slow-healing cuts, and poor appetite. Confusion, unsteady walking, or unusual eye movements in a heavy drinker need urgent care, because they can signal severe thiamine deficiency.
